text:
We have more planning engineers than ever. Every contract has a planning specification, DCMA checks and a monthly report template. So why are our projects still late?

The latest numbers:
• 79 % of the Middle East project professionals PwC surveyed said their projects were delayed in the past year, and 81 % reported cost overruns (PwC Middle East Capital Projects & Infrastructure Survey, 2025).
• On 2,410 projects in 122 countries that ended in claims or disputes, the extra time claimed averaged 66 % of the original schedule. In plain terms, a 24-month project asked for about 16 months more (HKA CRUX, 2026).
• Design failures drove the claims on 40 % of those projects: design errors (21 %), late design information (20 %) and incomplete design (17 %).
• Change in scope was the biggest single cause, on 33 %. In the Middle East it has been above 50 % (HKA CRUX, 2022).

Now look at where a planning team spends its month: collecting progress, updating P6, building the report.

The delay starts in design and in change. The planning effort goes into reporting construction. We are watching the wrong end of the project.

Design and scope change are planning problems, not only engineering and contract problems. This is what I believe planning has to take on, beyond reporting.

Design:
1. Put every drawing and vendor document in the schedule, tied by logic to the work it releases. Not "engineering 85 %".
2. Measure design maturity, not drawings issued. An IFC drawing with ten holds is not issued for construction.
3. Flag late or incomplete design the week it happens, with the construction date it moves.

Scope change:
4. Give every change a time impact the week it is raised, before it is approved. Not months later, in a claim.
5. Keep one change register, linked to the schedule, and review it in every progress meeting.
6. Show the client two dates: with the change and without it. Then let them decide.

IPA's research on more than 25,000 capital projects points the same way: how complete the front-end definition is, is the best single predictor of cost and schedule.

Reporting tells us how late we are. Planning the design and the changes is how we stop being late.

Planners: how much of your month goes on reporting, and how much on design and change?

What planning should do: not only report progress; plan the design and every scope change, with dates and owners.
